item.title: Red Hat Engineering Director Uses AI to Tackle Linux's Undocumented Driver Woes
Linus Torvalds' AI Code Improved: Performance Wins with Reworked Code
What is still hard to become good at as AI makes coding easier?
item.description:
Since LLMs came, how I build software changed for so many reasons. Since then, I’ve spent most of my time deciding what I want to build, how I want to build it, how I want to give the context, checking the result, seeing if there is an error, and paving the way for the LLM to do the right thing. And the difficult part, which is writing code and getting everything right, is handled by the LLM surprisingly well, from my work and the people around me and people who I look up to on the internet.

Until now, my edge was that you can get really far by understanding how computers work, like networking and CLI, kernels, reading errors, and following documents. You can get very far. But that strong edge is now fading because of how good LLMs are becoming lately. It won’t take that long. That edge would be gone when LLMs get much better at switching to the specific context of things. They still can do it, but you need to pave the way for them.

Now, people are saying you should have better judgment of what to develop for the future. But the issue is that I haven’t identified a hard thing worth committing to since LLMs came along.

I’m in my early career and trying to decide where I should invest my serious efforts. What capabilities remain difficult to acquire, are very niche, and aren’t something lots of people want to work on? There has to be something where human expertise remains valuable, including work where a human is still much cheaper than using LLMs.

I’m not looking for an answer like, “XYZ types of sites are very hard to build, and you should build one yourself and make money.” What I’m missing is a concrete problem, who needs it solved, what makes it difficult, and a path into working on it.

I’m not looking for an easy answer. I’m trying to see what you and other people have run into or understand about what’s going on right now. I need to find a hard thing to do, and I haven’t found one I feel confident committing to. Can you help me find one?

item.title: Loud, Fast, and Everywhere: Anatomy of a Real AI-Driven Cloud Attack
Show HN: Maali – Privacy-first personal finance app with a local AI analyst
item.description:
I never felt comfortable signing up for cloud budgeting apps and having them store all of my financial data on their servers. I also didn't find locally hosted options that I liked using.

That led me to build Maali (https://maali.app) over the past year. It is currently a Mac and Windows app that lets you track spending, budgets, recurring bills, income, net worth, and more. It stores all of your data on your computer.

You can bring your data in by either manually importing bank statement files (CSV/PDF), or by using SimpleFIN, a third-party bridge that you set up once and it keeps your data in sync. Since SimpleFIN introduces a third party that moves your data, I also added a power-user feature where Maali watches a folder (per account) and imports files dropped there, so you can automate downloads however you like and keep everything local.

It also has an optional AI analyst (local Gemma 4 E4B model) that provides commentary on your spending and flags anything unusual about your finances.

I realize that mobile is a big part of convenience for people. Maali lets you set up a phone web app over your own Tailscale network, paired by QR code. I'm also close to launching iOS/Android mobile apps that keep data in sync between the desktop/mobile apps using end-to-end encryption. My goal is to provide a great user experience with maximum convenience without sacrificing privacy.

The full app is free to use for 30 days (no card/signup needed). After that, if you find it useful and want to continue using it, it's $99 one-time. There's a live demo on the site (https://maali.app/today) with synthetic data so you can get a feel for it. Would love to hear any feedback that you have.

item.title: AI, Math, the Document-Drop. Non-Tech Thoughts
Show HN: Personal AI on your Mac – SuperDuck.AI (beta testers wanted)
item.description:
Personal AI has arrived, and it's now as easy as downloading a Mac app.

SuperDuck.AI runs the model on your own Mac. Your conversations, your files, your notes stay on your machine. No account, no cloud AI needed. There's an iPhone/iPad app that talks to your Mac over an end-to-end encrypted link, so your phone gets the same AI, with the Mac's files and web access, wherever you are.

Under the hood we bundle antirez's ds4 and other inference engines, so installing is one download and the models are files on your disk. The local model is an 80 GB download; several are supported and you pick in Settings. Apple Intelligence works as an engine too, if you'd rather not download a model at all.

For older or slower Macs there's an optional accelerated inference path through a LinuxToaster account, if you have one. It's a switch; off by default.

The harness around the model is ours: the model can't write a file, do a sum, keep the books or look something up without sending a command to the app, and everything it really did shows up as a under the reply. No , nothing happened, and the app says so.

We need beta testers for: - the Mac app (Apple silicon, 16 GB and up; 128 GB recommended for the local model) - the iPhone/iPad app - the harness itself: tell us when the model gets away with something

TestFlight links are at https://superduck.ai

Ask me anything about how it works.
